intro:
Zephaniah, the ninth of The Twelve (Minor Prophets), prophesies during Josiah's reign (640-609 BC), likely before the king's reforms. He's of royal descent (great-great-grandson of Hezekiah). His message: 'The great day of the Lord is near—a day of wrath, distress, anguish, ruin, darkness, gloom.'

Universal judgment announced: God will sweep away everything—Judah, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, Assyria (Nineveh specifically). Jerusalem especially condemned: 'The city of oppressors, rebellious and defiled!' Leaders, princes, prophets, priests all corrupt.

But after judgment, hope: 'Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land... perhaps you will be sheltered.' Remnant theme strong. Final chapter: God will restore fortunes, remove pride, leave humble people who 'will do no wrong.' Nations will worship together. 'I will give you honor and praise among all the peoples.'

Zephaniah's vivid imagery: 'Their blood will be poured out like dust... neither their silver nor gold will be able to save them.' Yet: 'The Lord your God is with you, the Mighty Warrior who saves. He will take great delight in you.'
outro:
Zephaniah presents the Day of the Lord as both terrifying judgment and hopeful purification. His preaching likely contributed to Josiah's reforms. The book moves from global wrath to specific hope for a remnant.

Key contribution: Emphasizes God's jealousy for pure worship and justice. The famous line 'He will rejoice over you with singing' shows God's emotional investment in His people.

Eschatological theme: The Day of the Lord isn't just historical but points to final judgment and restoration. Zephaniah influences later apocalyptic literature.

Modern relevance: Warning against complacency in religious privilege, hope for the humble, God's delight in redeeming a remnant.
